title: Making jazz understandable
summary: Responding to a remark from the first interview, Sportiello explains his goal of playing music that is beautiful, new and emotionally understandable even to non-musicians.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Yes. You know during our first interview you said something and I wrote it down, “to play jazz and make it understandable is one of my goals.” And it’s very curious that you’re actually able, in a different way, to accomplish that, the things you’re describing.

Well you know it’s almost a philosophical problem you know. How many times we listen, look at art and we don’t know what’s going on. We don’t. So it becomes sometimes a decision to say I like it or not. So sometimes we say I like it, sometimes we say I don’t like it, but we don’t have really a reason because we don’t really understand what is going on. And so I always wondered, is there a way to play music in my case, to play music and come up with something that can be beautiful, that can be smart, that can be also new but at the same time enjoyable and understandable. Understandable means even just, even if you’re not a musician, you don’t know about theory, you don’t have perfect pitch. But is there an emotion that goes through and gets to you. That’s, I think, what understandable means.
And so I’m constantly thinking of that. Every time I perform. Every time I make a recording or play live or make a post I ask myself will this communicate some sort of message? So I hope so.
